Kuwait: two Italian technicians killed by drones, Rome and Kuwait blame Iran, which denies it, Brussels wants to “increase the pressure” on Tehran

On Thursday, November 26, two Italian technicians from Rheinmetall Italia were killed in Kuwait during a drone attack on an air defense surveillance site. Kuwait and Italy blame Iran, which denies any involvement. They are among the first officially confirmed European deaths in the war with Iran [1][3].
The two men worked for Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian subsidiary of the German defense group Rheinmetall, at a Kuwaiti air defense detection station [1][3].

According to Kuwait, they were hit by debris while the army was trying to intercept drones coming from Iran [4]. Two other people were injured: a Pakistani national and a captain in the Kuwaiti army [2].

The Kuwaiti Defense Ministry speaks of a “vital site” targeted by an Iranian attack and denounces a “heinous Iranian aggression” [1][4]. The country had reactivated its air defenses a few days earlier, for the first time since early September [4].

Before the Italian Senate, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said that several Iranian-made drones had targeted Kuwaiti military installations [5]. Rome will lodge a protest with the Iranian embassy [1]. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her sorrow to the families [4].

The spokesman for the Iranian armed forces says Iran has carried out no military operation in the region and speaks of a “false flag” operation, without evidence [2][5]. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi phoned his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts to deny any role and propose a joint investigation [3][6].

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen responded: “We must increase the pressure on Iran to put an end to these unacceptable attacks against its neighbors and our Gulf partners” [7]. Rheinmetall did not comment [5].
Key takeaway: the war with Iran, which began in late February, is now killing Europeans in the Gulf, and the European Union is talking about taking a tougher line [3][7].

Kuwait, a small oil-rich emirate bordering Iraq and close to Iran, is on the front line: it had to switch its air defenses back on for the first time since September [4]. The victims were not soldiers but technicians from a private company responsible for maintaining the radars that protect the country [5].

The account remains disputed: Rome and Kuwait blame Tehran, while Iran denies it and accuses Israel and the United States of manipulation, without providing evidence [1][5]. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar sees it as proof that Iran's “unchecked aggression” threatens stability in the Middle East [4].
For Europe, the stakes are concrete: the Commission's call to “increase the pressure” may signal new sanctions against Iran [7].

If the European Union decides on new sanctions against Iran, this could push oil and gas prices up a little further. And if you work or travel in the Gulf, this tragedy is a reminder that Iran's neighbors are not safe.

news.2026-11-27-chine-profits-industriel: China: driven by AI and copper, factory profits jump 20% in October, but cars and furniture sink deeper

Profits at China's large industrial companies rose 20.1% year on year in October, their biggest increase since May, the National Bureau of Statistics announced on Friday, November 27. Electronics, boosted by demand linked to artificial intelligence, and metals are driving growth, while consumer-facing sectors are declining [1][2].

October's increase (+20.1%) is a clear acceleration from +14.4% in September [1]. Over the first ten months of 2026, profits reached 6,737.36 billion yuan, up 16.0%, compared with +15.5% over nine months [1][2].
The figure also benefits from a very low base of comparison: in October 2025, industrial profits had fallen 5.5%, their worst result in five months [4].

According to Yu Weining, the Bureau's chief statistician, electronics profits doubled over ten months, as AI computing needs are sending demand for memory chips soaring [3]. Profits of complete computer manufacturers jumped 410%, and those of special materials for electronics 220% [3].
High-tech industry as a whole posted +50.9% [1][2]. Rising copper and aluminum prices lifted profits in non-ferrous metal smelting by 71.7% and in mining of these metals by 60.2% [3].
Conversely, sectors that sell to households are suffering: furniture profits plunged 52.4% from January to October, and car industry profits fell 22.8% over the first nine months [1].
The firm Capital Economics estimates that China's GDP grew only about 2.4% year on year in October, compared with 3.5% in the first half [1].
Key takeaway: Chinese industry is moving at two speeds. Factories linked to AI and metals are making a lot of money, while those that depend on Chinese consumer spending are losing it [1][3].

This contrast reflects Beijing's strategy: betting on high technology and exports rather than domestic demand. It also shows its limits, because households buying less furniture and fewer cars slow down the whole economy, hence estimated growth of only 2.4% in October [1].

Part of the rebound comes from prices: when copper and aluminum rise, mines and smelters earn more, without the economy necessarily producing more [3]. And the comparison with a very poor October 2025 mechanically inflates the percentage [4].

The figure comes just as Washington wants to impose a 20% tariff on Chinese goods over “overcapacity,” meaning factories that produce more than the market can absorb: sharply rising industrial profits will not help Beijing argue otherwise [5].

When demand for memory chips explodes because of AI, these are the same components found in computers and phones: the Chinese boom shows that this rush is continuing [3]. And a China whose households consume little seeks to sell elsewhere, notably in Europe, which weighs on European manufacturers.

Mar-a-Lago: Trump and the NATO chief urge Russia not to widen the war, then Trump adds Ukraine to the warning

On Wednesday, November 25, Donald Trump hosted NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida. Their joint statement calls on Russia to avoid any action that would expand the war. But the version published by Trump also targets Ukraine, a discrepancy NATO has not explained [1][3].
The war between Russia and Ukraine and the war between the United States and Iran were the main topics of the meeting, according to the statement [4].
In NATO's version, the two leaders stress “the importance of Russia avoiding any action that, intentionally or not, widens the war” [1][2].

In his Truth Social post, Trump added Ukraine to this warning, which originally targeted only Moscow [3]. A NATO official told Politico that both sides had agreed on the original text; it is unclear which version is official [3].
The statement also welcomes the NATO summits in The Hague and Ankara. The two men discussed military spending, which Trump is pressing Europeans to increase [4].
Mark Rutte reiterated that any agreement must include security guarantees for Ukraine [5].
The meeting came after Trump's three-way summit with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, and a few hours before Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions [5].
Key takeaway: a single added word changes the meaning of the message. Warning Russia alone means naming the aggressor; warning Ukraine as well puts the two countries on the same footing [3].

NATO is the military alliance that binds the United States, Canada and most European countries. The fact that a joint statement exists in two different versions shows how hard Washington and the Europeans find it to speak with one voice on Ukraine [3][4].
The timing matters too. Russia struck Kyiv right after the meeting [5], and Trump keeps pressing Europeans to pay more for their defense [4].
The next day, in his Thanksgiving messages, Trump returned to his meeting with Mark Rutte and cited the destruction of Iran's navy and air force among his successes [6].

France is a member of NATO. If Washington treats Russia and Ukraine the same way, Europe will have to take on a larger share of support for Kyiv and of its own defense, and that is paid for with higher taxes and military budgets.

Taiwan votes on Saturday: 22 mayoral races at stake, investigations into interference and the first big test for Lai Ching-te against Beijing since 2024

On Saturday, November 28, Taiwanese voters elect the mayors and heads of the island's 22 cities and counties, as well as 919 councilors. This first major election since 2024 is being closely watched by Beijing, which is accused of trying to influence the vote, something it denies [3][4].

The Kuomintang (KMT), the opposition party that favors closer ties with China, currently runs 14 of the 22 local governments [4]. President Lai Ching-te's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) wants to win back ground [4].

In Taipei, a historic KMT stronghold, DPP candidate Puma Shen is challenging incumbent mayor Chiang Wan-an [4]. In New Taipei, the island's largest city, polls show Lee Shu-chuan (KMT) and Su Chiao-hui (DPP) neck and neck [4].

Taipei's two main candidates canceled their street rallies after a controversy over road closures that had blocked downtown traffic; they are campaigning online [2]. On Friday evening, Lai Ching-te and former president Tsai Ing-wen are due to back Puma Shen and Su Chiao-hui [1].
KMT chair Cheng Li-wun acknowledges tight races in Taipei, New Taipei, Taoyuan and Taichung, but says she is optimistic in all four cities [1].

Taiwan's criminal police are investigating around thirty cases of suspected foreign interference [3][5]. In October, Beijing's Taiwan Affairs Office sanctioned a company linked to Puma Shen's father, which Taipei's Mainland Affairs Council called electoral interference [6].

On Wednesday, November 26, Taiwan's coast guard launched patrols along the northern coast and the islands against smuggling and illegal entry; in the Penghu islands, four Chinese fishing boats were driven away [7].
Key takeaway: this local vote takes Taiwan's political temperature two years ahead of the 2028 presidential election, and Beijing will use it to assess its pressure strategy [4][8].

According to the American think tank CSIS, a strong KMT showing would be read by Beijing as a rejection of the DPP's line toward China [4]. A report by the US Congress commission on China says Beijing will watch this election to gauge whether pressure can bring the island closer to unification [8].
Yet mayors have no power over China policy, and the campaign has mostly focused on local issues, analysts point out [3]. Beijing denies any interference [3].
There is also a budget dimension: the result will weigh on the standoff between the Lai government and the opposition-controlled Parliament over defense spending [5].

Taiwan is a key link in the supply of the electronic chips found in your phone or your car. A vote that reassures or worries Beijing changes the level of tension in the region, and therefore the risk hanging over this production and over electronics prices in Europe.

Stellantis soars 8.9% in Paris: Brussels partly shuts the door on Chinese hybrids, Washington caps its tariffs at 15%

On Thursday, November 26, Stellantis gained 8.91% and Renault 5.74%, leading the CAC 40, which rose 1.61% to 8,108.74 points. European carmakers are benefiting from two pieces of news: European quotas on imported hybrid cars and US tariffs that are lighter than feared [1][2][3].

On Tuesday evening, November 24, the European Commission announced quotas on imported hybrid cars, from all origins, from December 1, 2026 to June 18, 2027. Beyond the quota, cars are blocked. China is allowed 191,780 vehicles over the period, Japan 170,889 [5].

Each exporting country gets its 2025 import volume, plus a little over 15%. Brussels considers that the sharp rise in imports poses an “imminent and serious” threat to European industry, partly because of global overcapacity [5].

On Wednesday, Volkswagen already gained nearly 6%, Stellantis 5.5% and BMW nearly 5% [4], Renault 4.9% to 28.08 euros [11]. Citi estimates that the quotas will deprive China of more than 500,000 sales in 2027, and that Renault will benefit the most [4].

On Thursday, the rebound gathered pace: investors were reassured by US tariffs that were lighter than feared [2]. Washington proposes to tax 14 economies for “overcapacity,” but promises to respect the 15% cap negotiated with the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, after a public hearing on January 25 [3].
In Frankfurt, the DAX gained 2.14%, driven by Porsche, Volkswagen and BMW [6]. In Paris, 39 of the 40 CAC 40 stocks rose, all except EssilorLuxottica [1].
Stellantis is starting from a very low level: 3.085 euros on Monday, November 23, and still more than 65% below its high for the year, 9.851 euros on January 5 [7].

Key takeaway: Europe is moving from tariffs to quotas to protect its car industry. In 2024, it had taxed Chinese electric cars [8]; Chinese brands then turned to hybrids, which those tariffs did not cover. The quota closes that loophole [5].

But the trap is for Europeans themselves: the quota counts the country where the car is made, not the brand [9]. Stellantis's Peugeot 208 hybrid is assembled in Kenitra and Renault's Dacia Jogger hybrid in Tangier, Morocco; both groups, like Nissan and Toyota, could be affected [13]. And Morocco is allowed only 23,954 hybrids over the period [12].
On the US side, nothing is applied yet: it is a proposal [3]. But the 15% cap removes the worst-case scenario, and on the stock market uncertainty often costs more than a known tax [2].

If you were planning to buy an imported Chinese or Japanese hybrid, supply could shrink from December 1 once the quotas are reached, and prices could fall less. If you have a PEA, Stellantis and Renault are part of the CAC 40 [1]: their shares remain very sensitive to decisions in Brussels and Washington.

How it works: why a quota lifts European carmakers

A tariff makes an imported car more expensive, but a very competitive seller can absorb the tax by cutting its margin. A quota, on the other hand, sets a maximum number: beyond it, the cars do not get in [5]. European competitors therefore know how many imported cars they will face, and can sell more, or cut their prices less. Investors anticipate higher profits and buy the stock. Here, it is a “safeguard” measure, allowed by world trade rules: Brussels does not have to prove an unfair practice such as dumping, only a sudden surge in imports that threatens its industry, and the measure is limited in time [10][5]. Why does Stellantis move so much? Its share is worth about 3.5 euros [1]: after a fall of more than 65% since January [7], the slightest good news triggers a wave of buybacks.
Precedents: the European car industry at the mercy of borders
October 30, 2024
The EU imposes five-year duties on Chinese electric cars: 17% for BYD, 18.8% for Geely, 35.3% for SAIC, 7.8% for Tesla and 20.7% for the others, on top of the usual 10% [8].
Chinese brands got around the tax by betting on hybrids, hence the 2026 quotas.
April 30, 2025
Stellantis suspends its 2025 targets because of US tariffs, after quarterly revenue fell 14% to 35.8 billion euros [14].
For a carmaker with a large US presence, tariff uncertainty makes it impossible even to forecast its results.
October 7, 2026
On a mere Bloomberg report that Brussels is considering limits on Chinese hybrids, Renault gains 4.38% to 26.91 euros and Stellantis 3.55% to 4.21 euros, leading the CAC 40 [10].
The market had already bet on the measure; Stellantis then fell back to 3.085 euros on November 23 [7], a sign that its problems go beyond China.

Indonesia: the rupiah falls to 18,400 to the dollar, an all-time low, despite a rate hike eight days ago

On Thursday, November 26, the Indonesian rupiah crossed 18,400 rupiah to the dollar, its weakest level in history. The central bank, Bank Indonesia, says it is intervening in all markets. It blames the US Fed, the threat of a downgrade of the Jakarta stock market by MSCI and corporate demand for dollars [1][2].

On Thursday, the rupiah briefly passed 18,400 rupiah to the dollar, its all-time low [1]. According to Bloomberg data cited by Katadata, this threshold was hit at 11:48 a.m. Jakarta time [4]. The day before, it had already closed at a record 18,303, down 0.53% [5].
According to Reuters, it lost as much as 0.5% during the day [12], and the central bank announced new interventions [3].

Erwin Gunawan Hutapea, head of monetary management at Bank Indonesia, cites three causes: expectations of a US rate hike, which strengthens the dollar; fears of a reclassification of the Indonesian stock market, which is driving capital away; and corporate dollar purchases before the end of the month [1].

The response: the bank is selling dollars on the spot market, using forward contracts settled in rupiah (“NDF”), including abroad, buying back government bonds and making sure banks have enough foreign currency [1].

On November 18, Bank Indonesia had already raised its key rate by 0.25 point, to 6% [6]. Only 10 of the 27 economists polled by Reuters expected it [7]. That makes a total increase of 1.25 points since the start of 2026 [7].

Governor Destry Damayanti then described it as a “preemptive” move ahead of a possible Fed rate hike in December [7]. Reuters also linked the rupiah's fall to the resignation of the vice president the previous week [7].

Key takeaway: Indonesia is paying both for the strong dollar and for doubts about the quality of its stock market. On October 15, index provider MSCI proposed moving it out of “emerging markets” into a “standalone” status [8]. On October 16, Indonesian stocks lost about 11%, their worst session in 28 years [9].

MSCI says it will go through with it “unless there is clear evidence of significant improvements” in market governance [8]. On November 24, it reiterated that nothing had changed, despite press reports to the contrary [10]. Yet many funds track these indices to the letter: if Indonesia drops out, they sell Indonesian stocks, then the rupiah they receive.

So the rate hike was not enough: the threat of funds pulling out weighs more heavily. If the pressure continues, the central bank will have to choose between drawing further on its reserves and raising rates again, at the risk of slowing the economy.

If you have an “emerging markets” or “Asia” fund in your PEA or life insurance policy, Indonesia still carries weight in it: an exit from the MSCI indices would force these funds to sell. For Indonesians, a weak rupiah makes everything paid in dollars more expensive, from fuel to corporate debt.

How it works: why a stock index can make a currency fall

MSCI does not set a country's policy: it sorts stock markets into categories (“developed,” “emerging”…) [8]. But thousands of funds copy these indices automatically. If Indonesia leaves the “emerging” category, these funds must sell its stocks, then exchange the rupiah they receive for dollars to bring the money home. These sales push the rupiah down. To defend it, the central bank sells part of its dollar reserves, which supports the exchange rate, and can raise its rates to make rupiah investments more profitable [1][6]. Here, the effect is amplified by the Fed: when US rates rise, the dollar attracts money from all over the world [1].
Precedents: the rupiah, a barometer of Indonesian crises
During the Asian financial crisis, the collapse of the rupiah triggers a financial crisis that helps end three decades of authoritarian rule by President Suharto [13].
In Indonesia, a currency crash can turn into a political crisis.
March 2020
At the start of the Covid-19 pandemic, the rupiah crosses the 16,000-to-the-dollar mark during trading, a level not seen since 1998, putting pressure on reserves and foreign-currency debt [14].
In global panics, money leaves emerging countries first.

After Donald Trump's tariff announcement, Bank Indonesia pledges to intervene “aggressively” [15]. On April 9, the rupiah falls to 16,957 during trading, below its 1998 low, before erasing its losses [11].
Interventions can slow a fall, but not reverse the trend when the dollar stays strong.
